name: Karl Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on a transmission construction crew, so we're building the big high-voltage lines, the ones on steel towers that bring power in from the wind farms up north. It's two weeks on, one week off, staying in a work camp or a motel near the site. A normal day is safety briefing at half six, then stringing conductor, bolting hardware on towers, or running the pulling rig with the crew. I love the scale of it, but two weeks away from home gets long.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home while you're away?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lena, my partner, she's a nurse at the regional hospital, so she works nights half the time anyway. We joke that we see each other more on video calls than in person. The money's very good with the travel allowance, and since I barely spend anything in camp, I've got about ten months saved. I'm still learning, though; the journeymen trust me with the rigging but not much higher up the tower yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the wind farm build-out matters way more to my job than any AI story. We're building lines because the grid has to grow, and that doesn't depend on chatbots. At camp I'd probably say good, now let's talk about the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means steady work for ten or fifteen years, as long as governments keep funding the grid. My worry was never AI. My worry is whether the next government cancels the renewable projects that keep our crews building. That's the thing that could actually stop our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on the apprenticeship and try to get my tower-climbing hours up so I can move off the ground faster. I'd keep using the AI quiz app now and then for my theory exams, because it's handy. And I'd keep putting money aside towards a flat with Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty settled, honestly. It's a good trade and it's a growing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the next government is the real risk. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Vote, obviously, and I'd go to the union's town hall before the election. Our local put out a campaign last time about keeping the grid projects public, and I handed out leaflets for an afternoon. I'm not a big activist, but that's the issue I'd show up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets bought first with the savings, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit on a flat near the hospital, so Lena's commute is short. We've looked at two already. In the plateau world I'd feel fine signing a mortgage next year.

say: I'd say the **grid build-out** matters far more to my job than any AI story.
I'd tell the camp it's good news and talk about the **next contract**.
think: Privately, the real risk is a **government cancelling** renewable grid projects, not AI.
This world means **steady work** for ten or fifteen years if funding holds.
do: Build up **tower-climbing hours** to move off the ground faster.
Keep using the **AI quiz app** now and then for theory exams.
Save towards a **flat deposit** near the regional hospital.
feel: He feels **calm** and settled in a growing trade.
S0.quote: My worry was never AI. My worry is whether the next government cancels the renewable projects that keep our crews building.
fieldNote: He ties his security to **public grid spending**, not technology.
He's a **light activist**: votes, leaflets, attends union town halls.
His main plan is a **mortgage** with his partner, which this world allows.

steps.text: Log more tower-climbing hours on the wind farm line
Put a deposit on a flat near the regional hospital
Hand out union leaflets about public grid projects before the election

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trades are the safe bet now, and I'd say it to anyone thinking about uni. At camp the talk would be about which office jobs are going. Online I'd share stuff about protecting the people who lose out, because it isn't their fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly fine. The planning and the design office might shrink, but someone still has to bolt the tower together and pull the wire. My worry would be Lena's side, the hospital admin, maybe some of the paperwork nurses do, though not the actual nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company if they're bringing in any new planning software, and I'd learn it early so I'm useful when it lands. I'd keep the flat plan going, maybe go for a slightly smaller place to be safe. And I'd stay active in the union, because when jobs shrink somewhere, someone has to fight for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy for friends in office jobs, but not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate from school does customer service for a phone company, and another one does bookings for a travel firm. Both of them are exactly the jobs on that card. I'd probably tell them to look at the trades, honestly, the line apprenticeship has a waitlist but it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go for a smaller flat. Why, if your job is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I suppose because nobody's sure how fast it moves, and a smaller mortgage means I sleep better. Lena would say I'm being careful for the sake of it, and she might be right.

say: I'd say **the trades** are the safe bet now, especially to anyone weighing up university.
Online I'd share calls to **protect people** who lose office jobs.
think: Privately, **bolting towers** and pulling wire stays human for a long while.
The risk sits with **office staff** and some hospital admin, not his crew.
do: Learn any new **planning software** early so he's useful when it lands.
Keep the **flat plan** but look at a slightly smaller place.
Stay active in the **union** to push for retraining for others.
feel: He's **mostly calm**, with a bit of unease for friends in office jobs.
S1.quote: Someone still has to bolt the tower together and pull the wire.
fieldNote: He points friends in **office jobs** towards a line apprenticeship.

steps.text: Learn the company's new planning software as soon as it arrives
Look at smaller flats to keep the mortgage lower
Push the union to fund retraining for laid-off office staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for workers right now, a proper one. Public money for retraining, slowing down how fast utilities can bring robots in, unions at the table. I'd be posting about that every day, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the first two years wouldn't touch my hands, but the robots in 2031 would. Tower work is repetitive in a way; same bolts, same hardware, every tower. I can picture a robot climbing and bolting faster than me, and I'd only be four years into the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the mortgage, straight away. I'd talk to the union about what our contract says about new equipment, and I'd start a short course on robotics maintenance at the technical college, the evening one. Lena and I would talk about whether she moves to a hospital job that's more patient-facing, safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got savings, so I'm not desperate, but two years then three is quick. I'd feel like I'd picked the right trade at the wrong time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that robotics course look like, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college has a twelve-week evening certificate in industrial robot maintenance. I'd do it on my week off, it's not ideal, but it's something. If robots are going up towers, someone has to service them, and I'd rather be that someone than nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Lena would change jobs. Is that her idea or yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mine, really, and I'd have to be careful how I say it. She's the one who knows the hospital, so it'd be a conversation, not me telling her. But the paperwork side of nursing is exactly what goes in 2028.

say: I'd demand a **worker plan** now: public retraining money and unions at the table.
I'd argue for **slowing utilities** from bringing robots in too fast.
think: Privately, **robots in 2031** could climb and bolt towers faster than him.
He'd only be **four years** into the trade when they arrive.
do: Put the **mortgage on hold** straight away.
Take an evening **robotics maintenance** certificate at the technical college.
Check what the **union contract** says about new equipment.
feel: He feels **anxious** but not desperate, thanks to ten months of savings.
He feels he picked **the right trade** at the wrong time.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd picked the right trade at the wrong time.
fieldNote: He sees **tower work** as repetitive enough for robots to master.
His **ten months saved** keep him from panic, but the mortgage goes on hold.
He talks about his partner's job change carefully, as **a conversation**.

steps.text: Put the flat mortgage on hold for now
Take the twelve-week evening robot maintenance certificate
Read the union contract's new-equipment clause with the steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get it right, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's coming. I'd want the union pushing for a retraining fund and a say in how robot crews get rolled out on transmission projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes me feel a lot better than two. I'd be a journeyman by then, with real experience. And the robots at 2034 would be landing when there's still a huge grid to finish, so I think there'd be work alongside them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the robotics certificate, but over a year instead of cramming it. I'd go ahead with a smaller flat, because I'd have a few years of solid pay ahead. And I'd use the AI tools more on purpose, for exam prep and maybe the tower drawings, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but I have time and a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger kid thinking of joining the line trade in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but learn the robots too, from day one. The line trade isn't going to vanish in five years. But the kid who can climb and also run the machine is the one who keeps working after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut, if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out on my week off, which is when Lena and I splurge. The savings stay put, though, I wouldn't touch those.

S3.quote: The kid who can climb and also run the machine is the one who keeps working after 2034.

He sees a long overlap where **people and robots** work together on grid projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Train apprentices in the robots from now, keep people on the crews, and make sure the grid gets built faster, not just cheaper. That's the line I'd take at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2036 I'd be ten years into the trade and maybe running a crew. The robots around 2039 would be a big shift, but I'd be thirty-nine with a lot of experience, and someone has to plan and supervise those jobs. Though AGI might plan them, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Lena, the normal-sized one. I'd take the robotics course at a relaxed pace and keep my options open. I'd also put a bit into a pension top-up, because ten years of good pay is a chance to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I feel I've got time to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You caught yourself there, about AGI planning the jobs. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just that the supervising part is thinking work, and that arrives in 2036. So the job I'd be aiming for, running a crew, is the part the AI does first. That's a bit of a twist, I hadn't thought of it till now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stay hands-on longer than I planned, not rush into supervising. The hands-on part lasts three more years, so that's the safer bit, funny enough.

I'd argue the grid should be built **faster, not just cheaper**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, then robots by 2031, when I'm barely four years in. What would help is the union having a real say, and public money for courses we can do on paid time, not just on our week off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families. Lineworkers on transmission are away half the month, and if the work changes, it changes home life too. Lena and I have built everything around my rotation.

headlineQuote: Lineworkers on transmission are away half the month, and if the work changes, it changes home life too.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old apprentice** on a transmission crew building tower lines from wind farms.
He works **two weeks on**, one off, and has saved about ten months of pay.
He uses **AI tools** now and then for exams and is a light union activist.
He sees the **grid build-out** as his real job security, more than any AI trend.
He grows **anxious** only in the fastest picture, where robots reach towers by 2031.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, with **robots by 2031** when he's four years in.
whatWouldHelp: A real **union say** and public money for courses on **paid time**.
